title: Truth is not condemned for being said plainly
source_text: Πρὸς τοῦτο δὴ καὶ πρὸς πάντα, ὅσα ἐκοινοποίησεν ὁ Κέλσος, μὴ δυνηθεὶς αὐτῶν ἀντιβλέψαι τῇ ἀληθότητι, φάσκων αὐτὰ καὶ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν εἰρῆσθαι, τοιαῦτα λεκτέον· εἰ ὠφέλιμόν ἐστι τὸ δόγμα καὶ τὸ βούλημα αὐτοῦ ὑγιὲς, εἴρηται δὲ Ἕλλησι μὲν παρὰ Πλάτωνι ἤ τινι τῶν Ἑλλήνων σοφῶν, Ἰουδαίοις δὲ παρὰ Μωϋσεῖ ἤ τινι τῶν προφητῶν, Χριστιανοῖς δὲ (ἐν) τοῖς ἀναγραφεῖσιν Ἰησοῦ λόγοις ἢ λελεγμένοις παρά τινι τῶν ἀποστόλων αὐτοῦ· οὐ νομιστέον κατηγορεῖσθαι τὸ λεγόμενον παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἢ παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς ἐκ τοῦ καὶ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν αὐτὰ εἰρῆσθαι, καὶ μάλιστα ἐὰν ἀποδεικνύηται τὰ Ἰουδαίων πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν. οὐδὲ πάλιν ὑπὸ τοῦ κάλλους τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς φράσεως λεγόμενον τὸ αὐτὸ πάντως κρεῖττον εἶναι νομιστέον τοῦ εὐτελέστερον ἀπαγγελλομένου καὶ ἁπλουστέραις λέξεσι παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἢ Χριστιανοῖς· καίτοι γε ἡ πρώτη Ἰουδαίων λέξις, ᾗ οἱ προφῆται χρησάμενοι καταλελοίπασιν ἡμῖν βιβλία. Ἑβραίων διαλέκτῳ καὶ σοφῇ συνθέσει τῶν ἐν τῇ διαλέκτῳ κατ᾿ ἐκείνους ἀναγέγραπται. εἰ δὲ χρὴ καὶ τὴν τῶν δογμάτων ταυτότητα, κἂν παράδοξος ὁ λόγος εἶναι δοκῇ, δεῖξαι βέλτιον εἰρημένην παρὰ τοῖς Ἰουδαίων προφήταις ἢ τοῖς λόγοις Χριστιανῶν, οὕτω τὸν λόγον κατασκευαστέον ἀπό τινος τοῦ περὶ τὰς τροφὰς καὶ τὴν σκευασίαν αὐτῶν παραδείγματος. ἔστω τι ὑγιεινὸν βρῶμα καὶ ἰσχύος τοῖς ἐσθίουσιν ἐμποιητικὸν. τοῦτο δὲ οὕτως μὲν σκευασθὲν καὶ τοιοῖσδε ἡδύσμασιν ἀρτυθὲν λαμβανέτωσαν οὐχ οἱ μὴ μανθάνοντες ἄγροικοι καὶ ἐν ἐπαύλεσιν ἀνατεθραμμένοι καὶ πένητες τὰ τοιάδε ἐσθίειν ἀλλ᾿ οἱ πλούσιοι καὶ ἁβροδίαιτοι μόνοι· οὐκ ἐκείνως δὲ καὶ ὡς δοκεῖ τοῖς νομιζομένοις καθαριωτέροις σκευασθὲν. ἀλλ᾿ ὡς μεμαθήκασιν ἐσθίειν οἱ πένητες καὶ οἱ ἀγροικότεροι καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐσθιέτωσαν μυριάδες ὅλαι. εἰ οὖν καὶ διδοῖτο ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς τοιασδὶ σκευασίας (τοὺς) νομιζομένους καθαριωτέρους μόνους ὑγιάζεσθαι. οὐδενὸς τῶν πολλῶν προσβάλλοντος τοῖς τοιοῖσδε βρώμασιν, ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς τοιασδὶ τὰ πλήθη τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὑγιεινότερον διάγειν· τίνας μᾶλλον τοῦ κοινωνικοῦ ἕνεκεν ἀποδεξόμεθα τῶν ὑγιεινῶν βρωμάτων χάριν; ἆρά γε τοὺς τοῖς λογίοις χρησίμως αὐτὰ σκευάζοντας ἢ τοὺς τοῖς πλήθεσι; τῆς ἴσης (δεδόσθω γὰρ) ὑγιείας καὶ εὐεξίας ἐγγινομένης ἀπὸ τῶν οὑτωσὶ σκευασθέντων ἢ οὑτωσὶ, ἀλλὰ φανερὸν ὅτι αὐτὸ τὸ φιλάνθρωπον καὶ τὸ κοινωνικὸν ὑποβάλλει κοινωφελέστερον εἶναι ἰατρὸν τὸν τῆς τῶν πολλῶν ὑγιείας προνοησάμενον ἤπερ τὸν τῆς ὀλίγων μόνων.
pass_a_gloss: To this then and to all that Celsus made common (κοινοποιέω), not having been able to look in the face (ἀντιβλέπω) their truth (ἀληθότης), saying them to have been said also among Greeks, such things must be said: if beneficial (ὠφέλιμος) is the doctrine (δόγμα) and its intent (βούλημα) sound (ὑγιής), and it has been said for Greeks by Plato or one of the Greek wise (σοφοί), for Jews by Moses or one of the prophets, for Christians in the recorded (ἀναγράφω) words (λόγοι) of Jesus or things said by one of his apostles, one must not think (νομιστέον) the thing said among Jews or Christians accused (κατηγορέω) from its also having been said among Greeks, and most of all if the things of the Jews are demonstrated (ἀποδείκνυμι) older (πρεσβύτερος) than the Greek. Nor again must one think the same thing, said with the beauty (κάλλος) of Greek phrasing (φράσις), wholly better (κρείττων) than what is reported more cheaply (εὐτελέστερον) and in simpler (ἁπλοῦς) words (λέξεις) among Jews or Christians; and yet the first diction (λέξις) of the Jews, which the prophets using have left us books, was written in the dialect (διάλεκτος) of the Hebrews and a wise composition (σοφὴ σύνθεσις) of the things in the dialect according to them (κατ᾿ ἐκείνους). But if one must also show the sameness (ταυτότης) of the doctrines, even if the statement seems paradoxical (παράδοξος), better said among the prophets of the Jews or the words of Christians, thus must the argument be built (κατασκευαστέον) from an example (παράδειγμα) about foods (τροφαί) and their preparation (σκευασία). Let there be some healthful food (ὑγιεινὸν βρῶμα), productive (ἐμποιητικός) of strength (ἰσχύς) for the eaters. Let this, prepared so and seasoned (ἀρτύω) with such seasonings (ἡδύσματα), be taken not by the rustics (ἄγροικοι) not learning to eat such things and raised in farmsteads (ἐπαύλεις) and poor (πένητες), but by the rich and delicately-living (ἁβροδίαιτοι) alone; but prepared not that way, and as seems good to those thought cleaner (καθαριώτεροι), but as the poor and the more rustic and the many of men have learned to eat, let whole myriads (μυριάδες) eat it. If then it were granted that from such a preparation only those thought cleaner are made healthy (ὑγιάζομαι), none of the many approaching (προσβάλλω) such foods, but from such another the multitudes (πλήθη) of men live (διάγω) more healthily: whom rather for the sake of the social (τὸ κοινωνικόν) shall we approve (ἀποδέχομαι) on account of the healthful foods? Those preparing them usefully for the learned (λόγιοι) or those for the multitudes? Equal (for let it be granted, δεδόσθω) health (ὑγίεια) and good condition (εὐεξία) arising from those prepared thus or thus, yet it is plain that the love of humankind (τὸ φιλάνθρωπον) itself and the social suggest (ὑποβάλλω) that more commonly beneficial (κοινωφελέστερος) is the physician (ἰατρός) who provided for (προνοέω) the health of the many than the one of only a few.
pass_b_english: To this, then, and to everything else that Celsus has treated as common property, saying that these things were said among the Greeks too, because he could not look their truth in the face, we must answer as follows. If a doctrine is beneficial and its intent sound, and it has been said among the Greeks by Plato or by one of the Greek sages, among the Jews by Moses or by one of the prophets, and among Christians in the recorded words of Jesus or in what was said by one of his apostles, we must not think that what is said among Jews or Christians stands condemned because the same things were said among the Greeks too; and least of all if the Jewish teachings are shown to be older than the Greek.

Nor again must we think that the same thing, said with the beauty of Greek diction, is in every way better than what is expressed more plainly and in simpler words among Jews or Christians. And yet the original wording of the Jews, which the prophets used in the books they have left us, was written in the Hebrew language and with an arrangement of words that is skilful by the standards of that language.

But if we must also show, though the claim may seem paradoxical, that the same doctrines are better expressed by the prophets of the Jews or in the words of Christians, the argument must be built from an example taken from foods and the way they are prepared. Let there be some wholesome food that gives strength to those who eat it. Suppose this food, prepared in one way and flavoured with certain seasonings, is eaten not by country people, raised on farmsteads and poor, who have not learned to eat such things, but only by the rich and those who live in luxury. And suppose that, prepared not in that way, nor as seems good to those reckoned more refined, but in the way the poor, the more rustic and the majority of men have learned to eat it, it is eaten by tens of thousands.

If, then, it were granted that from the one kind of preparation only those reckoned more refined are made healthy, while none of the many approach such foods, but that from the other the multitudes of men live in better health: which shall we approve the more, for the sake of the common good, on account of their wholesome foods? Those who prepare them usefully for the learned, or those who prepare them for the multitudes? Let it be granted that equal health and vigour come from food prepared in the one way or in the other; still it is plain that love for humankind itself, and concern for the common good, suggest that the physician who has cared for the health of the many is of more common benefit than the one who has cared for the health of a few only.

choices.choice: ἐκοινοποίησεν: ‘treated as common property’, that is, treated Christian teachings as shared with, and so drawn from, the Greeks. τὰ Ἰουδαίων πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν: neuter, ‘the things of the Jews’; rendered ‘the Jewish teachings’ to follow δόγμα in the same sentence (it could also mean their writings); this is Origen’s usual argument from the antiquity of Moses. κατ᾿ ἐκείνους: ‘by the standards of that language’ (literally ‘according to them’), meaning that the plainness Greeks see belongs to translation, not to the Hebrew. Koetschau’s supplements (ἐν) and (τοὺς) accepted. The two preparations are set out with imperatives (λαμβανέτωσαν, ἐσθιέτωσαν), rendered ‘suppose’. μυριάδες ὅλαι: ‘tens of thousands’ (literally ‘whole myriads’). λόγιοι: ‘the learned’. τὸ κοινωνικόν: ‘the common good’ (the social bond between people). No Scripture quoted.
ἐκοινοποίησεν: 'made out to be common property' -> 'treated as common property'
ἡ πρώτη Ἰουδαίων λέξις: 'original diction' -> 'original wording'
first preparation reordered so the relative clause follows its noun: 'country people, raised on farmsteads and poor, who have not learned to eat such things'
ἐσθιέτωσαν μυριάδες ὅλαι: 'whole multitudes' -> 'tens of thousands', kept distinct from πλήθη 'multitudes'; sentence recast so 'prepared ... but in the way' modifies the food
